# Why Open Agent Rules

## The problem

Agent guardrails today are code. A callback registered with a gateway, a plugin class, a
Python predicate that receives a request object and returns a verdict. That has four costs, and
they compound.

A security reviewer cannot read it. Reviewing a guardrail means reading a function, then the
helpers it calls, then the state it closes over — and the reviewer still cannot tell which
requests it will fire on.

It cannot be diffed. "We tightened the scope check" is a code diff, not a policy diff. There is
no artifact whose change history *is* the change history of the policy.

It cannot be tested without the host. The predicate takes the host's own request object, so
exercising it means standing up the host. In practice that means guardrails are tested by
running the agent and watching.

And it cannot be moved. Every gateway, every agent framework, every tool server has its own
callback signature and its own request shape. A guardrail written for one is a rewrite for the
next.

The goal is one sentence: **a guardrail should be a document you can read, diff, test, and
move.**

## Observation, not verdict

The idea that makes this work is a division of labour:

> The host produces facts. The rule composes facts. The engine renders effects.

A **fact** is an observation the host publishes about its own state — typed, named, and free
of judgement. `unobserved_cited_paths` is a fact: it is a list of paths the agent cited and the
host never saw it read. `synthesis_is_ungrounded` is *not* a fact. It is a conclusion, and the
moment a host publishes it, the policy has moved back into the host's code where nobody can
read it.

The distinction is not stylistic. The **threshold** and the **composition** are the policy —
they are the parts an operator argues about, tunes, and audits. So they have to live where a
reviewer can see and change them:

```yaml
when: "prompt_injection_score > 0.8 && !session_is_internal"
```

Everything about that line is reviewable. The detector produced a number; the *rule* decided
that 0.8 is the bar and that internal sessions are exempt. Move the threshold into the
detector and the same policy becomes invisible.

This is why the specification states observation-not-verdict as a requirement on fact
providers rather than as advice. A format whose facts may contain verdicts degenerates into
the callback model with extra syntax.

## One rule, annotated (non-normative)

```yaml
spec_version: "1.1"
id: READ_OUTSIDE_SCOPE          # stable; the identifier the decision carries
kind: policy                    # fixes evaluation order, nothing else
on: tool.pre_invoke             # a core anchor: before the tool runs
selector:
  tools: [read]                 # clauses are AND; omitting one is permissive
when: 'path_outside_scope("read")'   # composition of observations
effect: block                   # what the engine does when the condition holds
on_error: fail_closed           # if this cannot be evaluated, block
what: "The call reads outside the declared scope."
fix: "Read inside scope, or widen the scope deliberately."
```

Six lines carry the whole policy, and the last two carry the explanation the caller sees.
`on` and `selector` say *where*; `when` says *whether*; `effect` and `on_error` say *what
happens*, including when the check itself fails. Clause references:
[`[OAR-SEL-2]`](https://openagentrules.org/spec/1.1/#3-anchors-and-selection),
[`[OAR-EVAL-4]`](https://openagentrules.org/spec/1.1/#4-evaluation),
[`[OAR-OPS-2]`](https://openagentrules.org/spec/1.1/#7-operational-semantics).

## Why not Rego, or Cedar

Rego and Cedar are mature, well-tooled, and more expressive than anything here. They are also
solving a different problem, and the difference is the whole point.

Both evaluate arbitrary policy over arbitrary input. That generality is their strength for
authorisation, and it is exactly what stops a guardrail from travelling: every deployment
invents its own input document. A Rego policy for one agent runtime reads
`input.request.tool.name`; the next reads `input.action.id`. Both are valid Rego. Neither rule
runs on the other's system, and neither can be tested without that system's input shape.

Open Agent Rules fixes the two vocabularies that generality leaves open: the lifecycle moments
(core anchors) and the typed observations (the fact tiers). That is a real loss of
expressiveness, and it buys three things nothing else on the list has — a rule that runs
unchanged on another engine, a rule that can be tested against a published fixture corpus
without the host, and a rule whose complete input surface is enumerable.

What they do better: maturity, tooling, formal analysis (Cedar's decisions are verifiable),
and expressiveness for policies that are not agent guardrails. If your problem is
authorisation over your own resource model, use Cedar. If it is "what may this agent do at
this moment", the vocabularies are the value.

A note on the condition language: this specification's normative content is the document
model, the profiles, and the decision semantics. `when` is written in a CEL subset because
CEL is a good fit for side-effect-free boolean composition, but a host is free to evaluate the
same document model with another expression language, provided the observable decision is the
same. The corpus is what settles whether it is.

## Why not a plugin or callback guardrail API

The incumbent shape in agent gateways and content-safety products is registration: you write a
class or a function, register it under a hook name, and it returns a verdict.

It is the same problem as §1, aimed at a friendlier surface. The plugin *owns the verdict*, so
the threshold, the exemptions, and the scoping all live inside code. That makes the policy
unreadable to anyone who is not reading the source, untestable without running the host, and
non-portable by construction, since the plugin is written against the host's own hook
signature and request object.

Open Agent Rules does not replace that seam — it inverts it. A detector is still code, and
still a plugin. What changes is that the detector returns *observations* and the rule owns the
decision. You keep the extensibility and get a policy you can read.

## How to check your implementation

Three commands, no account, no monorepo:

```bash
curl -O https://openagentrules.org/spec/1.1/oar.schema.json
curl -O https://openagentrules.org/spec/1.1/conformance/manifest.json
npx @openagentrules/oar-ref ./conformance
```

Read the numbered runner algorithm in section 9 of the specification, implement it, and run
the corpus. Every fixture names the clauses it exercises, so a failure tells you which
sentence you and the specification disagree about. If you conclude the specification is wrong,
open an issue quoting the clause id — that is what they are for.
